newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court leaves human rights issues beyond EU scope to states.
newsitem.headline: Court leaves human rights issues beyond EU scope to states.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday it does not have jurisdiction to determine if national legislation outside the scope of Community law complies with the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights.
The Strasbourg Court of Human Rights ruled that a retired Austrian judge, Friedrich Kremzow, was sentenced to life for murdering an Austrian attorney without a fair trial.
Kremzow was not present when the Austrian court reviewed his sentence, increased it from 20 years to life, and decided to commit him to a regular prison and not a psychiatric hospital.
The Strasbourg court awarded Kremzow 230,000 Austrian schillings and Kremzow is now seeking to enforce that award in an Austrian court.
Kremzow argued that his right to freedom of movement under Community law was infringed by an unlawful penalty of imprisonment and that the member state responsible must be liable for damages.

The court said that although it respects and ensures fundamental rights to EU citizens, and recognizes the Convention as a significant document in protecting those rights, the court cannot give guidance to national courts on issues falling outside the scope of Community law.
Kremzow "is an Austrian national whose situation is not connected in any way with any of the situations contemplated by the treaty provisions on free movement of persons," the court said.

Where national legislation is concerned with a situation which, as in the case at issue in the main proceedings, does not fall within the field of application of Community law, the Court cannot, in a reference for a preliminary ruling, give the interpretative guidance necessary for the national court to determine whether that national legislation is in conformity with the fundamental rights whose observance the court ensures, such as those deriving in particular from the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.
